slides.heading: Find Closest Value In Bst
slides.subtitle: AlgoExpert · Easy · Binary Search Trees
slides.narration: Let's solve Find Closest Value In Bst, an easy binary search trees problem. We'll restate the problem, build the intuition, walk through the approach, read the Java solution, and finish with its complexity.

slides.heading: The problem
bullets: Return the value in the BST closest to the target (assume one answer).
Iteratively walk down, pruning half the tree each step.
slides.narration: Here's the problem. Return the value in the BST closest to the target (assume one answer). Iteratively walk down, pruning half the tree each step.

slides.heading: Intuition
bullets: The BST ordering lets us discard half the tree at every step, just like binary search.
slides.narration: The BST ordering lets us discard half the tree at every step, just like binary search.

slides.heading: Brute force vs optimal
bullets: Brute force: visit every node → O(n)
Optimal: follow the BST ordering → O(log n) average
Worst case O(n) on a skewed tree
slides.narration: Brute force visits every node and tracks the closest, which is linear. Using the BST property, each comparison discards an entire subtree, so on a balanced tree we only walk one root-to-leaf path, log n on average.

slides.heading: Approach
bullets: 1. Start at the root, tracking the closest value
2. Update closest if this node is nearer
3. Go left if the target is smaller, right if larger
4. Stop on an exact match or a null child
slides.narration: Step by step. First, start at the root, tracking the closest value. Second, update closest if this node is nearer. Third, go left if the target is smaller, right if larger. Fourth, stop on an exact match or a null child.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: At 10: closest so far 10; 12 > 10 → go right
slides.narration: At node 10, the closest value so far is 10. The target 12 is larger, so we go right and ignore the other subtree.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: At 15: closest so far 10; 12 < 15 → go left
slides.narration: At node 15, the closest value so far is 10. The target 12 is smaller, so we go left and ignore the other subtree.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: At 13: closest so far 13; 12 < 13 → go left
slides.narration: At node 13, the closest value so far is 13. The target 12 is smaller, so we go left and ignore the other subtree.

slides.heading: Java solution
slides.narration: We start at the root with the closest set to its value. In the loop we update closest if this node is nearer, then move left if the target is smaller, right if it's larger, and return immediately on an exact match.

slides.heading: Complexity
bullets: Time: O(log n) avg, O(n) worst
slides.narration: Time is O of log n avg, O of n worst. Space is constant.

slides.heading: Edge cases & pitfalls
bullets: Use absolute difference; watch integer overflow
slides.narration: Stop early on an exact match. On a skewed tree the path can be n long. And compute differences carefully if values are near the integer limits.

slides.heading: Interview tips & follow-ups
bullets: Prefer the iterative version: O(1) space
slides.narration: Mention that the iterative version uses constant space while recursion uses the call stack. A follow-up is finding the k closest values.

slides.heading: Recap
bullets: The BST ordering lets us discard half the tree at every step, just like binary search.
Complexity: O(log n) avg, O(n) worst
